blogs.title: One DuPont Standard Fits All: How Apex Bank v. CC Serve Reinforces Consistency Across Likelihood‑of‑Confusion Factors
blogs.description: This post dissects the Federal Circuit’s insistence that once similarity is established under the second DuPont factor it must be applied uniformly to the other factors—especially the sixth. We examine prior cases where inconsistent standards were struck down, unpack the court’s reasoning that the Board inventively narrowed similarity only for factor six, and consider how this decision may force TTAB examiners and practitioners to adopt a more holistic analysis rather than treating each factor in isolation.

blogs.title: When Do Third‑Party Marks Signal Weakness? Decoding the Sixth DuPont Factor After Apex Bank
blogs.description: The opinion vacates the Board’s conclusion that nine Aspire‑related credit‑card marks are insufficient to show weakness. We explore what constitutes “considerable” or “ubiquitous” use under Jack Wolfskin and Juice Generation precedents, assess how the court calibrated quantitative thresholds versus qualitative market presence, and offer practical guidance for gathering third‑party evidence when arguing that a senior mark is commercially weak.

blogs.title: Credit Cards versus Banking Services: Are They ‘Legally Identical’? Dissecting Factor Two in Apex Bank
blogs.description: Here we analyze the Court’s affirmation that credit‑card services are legally identical—in part—to banking and financing services for purposes of likelihood‑of‑confusion analysis. The discussion covers statutory definitions, the impact of the USPTO’s removal of "credit card services" from the ID Manual, and compares this reasoning with earlier circuit opinions that kept those categories separate. We also consider strategic implications for future disputes in overlapping financial sectors.

blogs.title: De Novo Review Meets Substantial Evidence: Procedural Insights from Apex Bank v. CC Serve
blogs.description: This article breaks down the Federal Circuit’s application of de novo review to TTAB legal conclusions while applying a substantial‑evidence standard to factual findings across the DuPont factors. We explain how appellate courts balance these standards, what it means for litigants contesting TTAB decisions, and whether this opinion signals a trend toward heightened scrutiny of Board fact‑finding in trademark oppositions.
